opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I've thought about this a lot, because I've had many conversations with economists and others who find explosive-growth arguments unpersuasive. I don't think the disagreement is mainly about any single parameter. It's more that the two camps are working from different reference classes and different intuitions about what the default should be.

If you're an economist, you've spent your career watching very impressive technologies arrive: electricity, computers, the internet. Each time there were people saying "this changes everything," and each time, frontier growth stayed stubbornly around two percent a year. So your prior, quite reasonably, is that any new technology gets absorbed into that steady trend. The burden of proof sits heavily on anyone claiming this time is different, and an argument that relies on a chain of somewhat speculative steps doesn't feel like it clears that bar.

Then there's bottlenecks. Even if AI gets very good at cognitive work, the slower-growth view says the economy is full of things AI can't immediately speed up: physical experiments, building factories, regulatory approval, human preferences and trust, energy and materials. In a Baumol-style picture, the parts you can't automate come to dominate, so even dramatic improvements in some sectors yield modest aggregate gains. To someone holding that view, the fast-growth story seems to wave away the messy, slow, physical, institutional world.

From my side, the core argument is that AI is not like previous technologies, because it can substitute for the thing that has always been the scarce input to innovation and growth, which is human minds. Historically, growth accelerated over thousands of years partly because more people meant more ideas, which meant more output, which meant more people. That feedback loop broke when fertility decoupled from income. AI could restore it: more output means more compute, which means more "researchers" and "workers," which means more output. If you take that seriously, the two-percent era looks less like a law of nature and more like a temporary regime.

But I think the honest reason people stay unconvinced is that this argument is fairly abstract, and it asks you to extrapolate to systems that don't exist yet. When you say "imagine AI that can do essentially everything a human worker can do, including physical work through robotics," a lot of skeptics either don't really believe that's coming soon, or they quietly substitute in a weaker version, something like a very good tool rather than a full substitute for labor. Once you do that substitution, slower growth is just the right conclusion. So a lot of the apparent disagreement about economics is really disagreement about capabilities and timelines that never gets surfaced.

There's also a social, vibes-level piece. Predicting thirty-percent annual growth sounds unhinged in most professional contexts. Being wrong in the conservative direction rarely costs anyone their reputation, whereas being wrong in the dramatic direction makes you look naive. So there's an asymmetry in who feels comfortable stating which views.

What I'd love to see, and what I've tried to push on, is getting both sides to name in advance what evidence would move them. If skeptics think physical bottlenecks will bind, what would we observe if they weren't binding? If people like me expect acceleration, what early indicators should show up in the next few years, and what do we concede if they don't? I think that's much more productive than trading priors back and forth.

r001.rationale: It says skeptics have seen past technologies billed as transformative while frontier growth stayed near 2%, so they treat rapid-growth forecasts as another claim that may not pan out.

r002.rationale: It says skepticism comes from a reasonable prior and a high burden of proof, and that a speculative chain may not clear that bar, rather than pointing to a specific flaw.

r003.rationale: It attributes to the slower-growth view the belief that physical and institutional bottlenecks constrain growth, and says the fast-growth story appears to wave away those constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on, and I want to be fair to the slow-growth camp because I think a lot of their reasons are actually pretty reasonable.

The first is just a base rate argument. If you look at the history of the last couple hundred years, growth has been remarkably steady at roughly two or three percent per year in frontier economies. And every previous technology that people thought would be transformative, electricity, computers, the internet, showed up in the growth statistics as, at best, a modest bump. So when someone comes along and says this time we're going to get ten or twenty or thirty percent growth, the natural reaction is, okay, people have said that before about other technologies, and they were wrong. Why should I believe you now?

The second thing, and I think this is the deeper disagreement, is that economists who are skeptical tend to think about the economy as being made up of many different tasks and sectors, and they emphasize that growth is bottlenecked by the slowest-moving parts. This is the Baumol effect idea. Even if you make some sectors enormously more productive, the stuff you can't automate, or the stuff that's constrained by physical processes, regulation, permitting, human preferences for human-provided services, that stuff comes to dominate your spending and your measured growth. So they'll say, sure, AI might make software or research way cheaper, but you still have to build the factories, you still have to run the clinical trials, you still have to get the permits, and all of that takes time.

And I think the fast-growth people, myself included, mostly agree that those bottlenecks are real. Where we disagree is on how binding they are once you have AI systems that are genuinely substitutes for human labor across essentially all cognitive tasks, including the task of figuring out how to get around bottlenecks. The historical analogies don't really cover that case. Electricity didn't go out and lobby for its own permitting reform or design its own factories. So I think the fast-growth argument really hinges on this one claim about broad substitutability, and if you don't buy that claim, or you think it's decades away, then the whole case falls apart and you're back to the base rates.

The third thing I'd mention is more sociological. A lot of the fast-growth arguments have come from people in the AI world, or people adjacent to it, and I think economists reasonably discount arguments from folks who have a stake in the technology being a big deal and who haven't engaged much with the growth literature. There's also a kind of vibe mismatch, where the fast-growth people are reasoning from first principles about what a system that can do anything a human can do would imply, and the economists are reasoning from data and from models that were calibrated on a world where that system didn't exist. Those two groups just find each other's style of argument unconvincing, and I don't think that's going to resolve until we see more empirical evidence one way or the other.

So I'd summarize it as: they're not unconvinced because they're being stubborn, they're unconvinced because the fast-growth case requires you to believe something pretty extraordinary about the technology, and until you believe that, every other part of the argument looks like wishful extrapolation.

r001.rationale: The response says skeptics see rapid-growth forecasts as repeating past claims about transformative technologies that did not produce large growth increases.

r002.rationale: It describes historical base rates as a reason for skepticism, but does not clearly say that this prior sustains skepticism even when no flaw in the AI-growth argument is identifiable.

r003.rationale: It says skeptics emphasize bottlenecks and slow-moving sectors, but does not say they believe mechanistic acceleration scenarios systematically underestimate those bottlenecks.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that people have different pictures of what the bottlenecks are. If your picture is that AI is another very useful technology, then you naturally look at previous technologies and say, “Electricity was hugely important, computers were hugely important, and neither of those caused the economy to grow ten times faster. Why should this be different?” And I think that’s a reasonable starting point.

The reason I take much faster growth seriously is that AI could substitute for the human effort that goes into inventing and deploying new technologies. In that case, you’re not just getting a better tool. You’re potentially getting a feedback loop where more AI helps you make better AI, and also helps you expand the rest of the economy, which lets you produce still more AI.

But that argument depends on how much of that process you can actually automate. Someone who expects slower growth might say, “Okay, you can do the research faster, but you still have to build the factory. You still have to run the experiment. You still have to get permission to build things.” If those complementary tasks remain slow, making the cognitive work much cheaper might not translate into dramatically faster growth.

So I think the disagreement is partly about whether we’re talking about AI that helps humans do their jobs or AI that can replace human labor across a very broad range of tasks. And then, even conditional on the latter, there’s a real disagreement about how binding the remaining physical and institutional bottlenecks will be. Historical experience is much more informative about the first case than the second, but the second also requires extrapolating into a world we haven’t observed.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI with electricity and computers, which did not make the economy grow ten times faster. It does not say slower-growth advocates see rapid-growth forecasts as another historically mistaken technological-revolution prediction.

r002.rationale: The response presents historical experience as a reasonable starting point, but does not state that this prior sustains skepticism even when no flaw in the AI-growth argument is identifiable.

r003.rationale: The response notes possible physical and institutional bottlenecks, but does not attribute to slower-growth advocates the claim that mechanistic acceleration scenarios systematically underestimate them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that the argument for much faster growth asks you to imagine a pretty big break from how the economy has worked historically. If you’ve spent a lot of time looking at economic growth, you’ve seen lots of technologies that were described as transformative, and then their effects showed up gradually. So there’s a reasonable instinct to ask, “Why would this be different?”

The reason I think it could be different is that AI could automate the process of coming up with and implementing new technologies, including improvements to AI itself. That’s different from making one particular industry more productive. But how much that matters depends on what remains a bottleneck. If you still need humans to make key decisions, or physical experiments take a long time, or deploying anything requires years of institutional change, then having much more cognitive labor might not translate into dramatically faster growth.

So I suspect some of the disagreement is about whether those bottlenecks are fundamental or whether sufficiently capable AI could work around them. And some of it is just that we don’t have a historical example of broadly substituting for human cognitive labor. People are bringing different intuitions to a situation where the historical evidence is necessarily pretty indirect.

r001.rationale: The response says people have seen technologies described as transformative whose effects arrived gradually, which can prompt them to ask why AI-driven growth would be different.

r002.rationale: It describes a historically grounded instinct for skepticism, but does not say that this prior sustains skepticism even when no flaw in the AI-growth argument can be identified.

r003.rationale: The response discusses possible bottlenecks and differing views about whether AI could work around them, but does not attribute to slower-growth advocates a belief that acceleration scenarios systematically underestimate bottlenecks.
